title: Jurisdiction and Powers of High Courts

blocks.content: The writ jurisdiction of the High Court under Article 226 is wider than that of the Supreme Court under Article 32 because it extends to both fundamental rights and ordinary legal rights.

rows: Enforcement of Fundamental Rights and ordinary legal rights
Applicable across the entire territory of India
Limited to the State territorial limits or cause of action

items: Article 226 is discretionary and covers ordinary legal rights, whereas Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right limited strictly to Part III rights.
High Court judges are appointed by the President, but can only be removed through a process similar to the removal of a Supreme Court judge.
Supervisory power under Article 227 covers both administrative and judicial superintendence over subordinate courts.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The High Court exercises original, appellate, supervisory, and writ jurisdictions under Part VI of the Indian Constitution.
Under Article 226, High Courts have the power to issue writs for both Fundamental Rights and legal rights.
High Courts act as Courts of Record under Article 215, giving them the authority to punish for contempt of court.
Supervisory jurisdiction under Article 227 grants High Courts power over all courts and tribunals throughout their territorial jurisdiction.
Parliament has the constitutional power to establish a common High Court for two or more states or Union Territories under Article 231.
